_comment: Batch 03 (Sets 4-5). Distractor-only rewrites to remove the longest-answer cue. Correct options, stems, and rationales are unchanged; each distractor keeps its original meaning and stays wrong for the same reason.

RN-S04-01.B: A client with hypothyroidism who reports constipation for 3 days and is asking for a stool softener before breakfast
RN-S04-01.C: A client with Cushing's syndrome who is asking about weight-loss options and wants to speak with a dietitian today
RN-S04-01.D: A client with type 2 diabetes whose pre-lunch glucose is 182 mg/dL and who reports feeling well and is ready to eat

RN-S04-02.A: Inject air into both vials, draw up the NPH insulin first, then draw up the regular insulin
RN-S04-02.C: Draw up the regular insulin, then inject it into the NPH vial, mix gently, and withdraw the combined dose
RN-S04-02.D: Draw up each insulin in a separate syringe, then transfer both doses into a third syringe to combine them

RN-S04-04.B: Administer glucagon 1 mg IM into the deltoid and recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
RN-S04-04.C: Give a peanut butter sandwich and a glass of milk, then recheck the glucose in 1 hour
RN-S04-04.D: Notify the provider of the glucose result and wait for prescriptions before treating

RN-S04-05.A: Place 15 g of glucose gel between the client's cheek and gum
RN-S04-05.C: Give 4 oz (120 mL) of orange juice through a straw
RN-S04-05.D: Administer the client's regular insulin subcutaneously

RN-S04-07.A: Doubling the metformin dose the day before the scan to keep the blood glucose well controlled during the fasting period
RN-S04-07.C: Giving the usual metformin dose with the contrast injection to prevent hyperglycemia while the client is NPO
RN-S04-07.D: No change to the metformin, which the client should keep taking twice daily with breakfast and dinner as usual

RN-S04-08.A: Blood glucose of 320 mg/dL measured on the bedside glucometer on admission to the unit
RN-S04-08.B: Kussmaul respirations with a fruity odor on the breath and a respiratory rate of 30/min on arrival
RN-S04-08.D: Arterial pH of 7.10 with a serum bicarbonate of 12 mEq/L and an elevated anion gap

RN-S04-09.A: Incisional pain rated 4 on a 0–10 scale when swallowing
RN-S04-09.C: Mild hoarseness when the client speaks after extubation
RN-S04-09.D: Small amount of serosanguineous drainage on the dressing

RN-S04-12.B: Oral fludrocortisone with a full glass of water
RN-S04-12.C: IV potassium chloride 20 mEq over 2 hours
RN-S04-12.D: Fluid restriction to 1,000 mL per day

RN-S04-14.A: "I'll take my dose in the morning with food to protect my stomach."
RN-S04-14.C: "I'll check my blood sugar as instructed and report high readings."
RN-S04-14.D: "I'll avoid people who are sick and wash my hands often."

RN-S04-16.A: Urine specific gravity decreases from 1.004 to 1.001 over the first day
RN-S04-16.C: Serum sodium increases from 148 to 154 mEq/L after the first dose
RN-S04-16.D: The client reports increased thirst and drinks more water at night

RN-S04-18.B: Restrict fluids to 1,000 mL/day to reduce the workload on the kidneys
RN-S04-18.C: Encourage bed rest to conserve energy while calcium levels are high
RN-S04-18.D: Provide a high-calcium diet with milk, cheese, and yogurt each day

RN-S04-19.A: Mild nausea during the first few weeks of treatment
RN-S04-19.B: Decreased appetite and eating smaller portions at meals
RN-S04-19.D: Feeling full sooner at meals and eating less than usual

RN-S05-07.A: Irrigate the catheter with 50 mL of sterile saline to clear any fibrin clot that may be blocking the dialysate outflow
RN-S05-07.C: Increase the dextrose concentration of the next exchange to pull more fluid into the peritoneal cavity
RN-S05-07.D: Remove the peritoneal dialysis catheter and notify the provider that the catheter is not functioning

RN-S05-13.B: Cola-colored urine, hypertension, periorbital puffiness, and a sore throat 2 weeks ago
RN-S05-13.C: Flank pain, fever of 102°F (38.9°C), and white blood cell casts in the urine
RN-S05-13.D: Polyuria with low urine specific gravity of 1.003 and excessive thirst

RN-S05-17.A: Urinary frequency every 30 to 60 minutes today
RN-S05-17.B: Burning and stinging pain on urination
RN-S05-17.D: Cloudy urine with a strong, foul odor

RN-S05-19.A: Restrict fluids for 12 hours before the scan to reduce the risk of fluid overload
RN-S05-19.C: Give a high-protein meal so the client is not fasting while having the scan
RN-S05-19.D: Administer a potassium supplement to replace electrolyte losses before the scan

PN-S04-01.B: Deciding how much sliding-scale insulin to give based on the resident's glucose result
PN-S04-01.C: Administering a resident's scheduled insulin dose before breakfast is served
PN-S04-01.D: Reinforcing insulin injection teaching with a resident who is newly diagnosed

PN-S04-03.A: "Use the exact same spot for every injection so the insulin is absorbed at the same rate every single time."
PN-S04-03.C: "Inject into your thigh right before you go jogging so the insulin starts working faster."
PN-S04-03.D: "Massage the site well for a minute after each injection to help the insulin spread out."

PN-S04-04.A: "Store both your opened and unopened vials together in the freezer, and thaw each one before you use it."
PN-S04-04.C: "Keep all of your insulin in the glove compartment of your car so that you always have a dose with you when you're out."
PN-S04-04.D: "Opened vials never expire, so you can keep using the same vial for as long as it takes to finish it."

PN-S04-09.A: "It shows that your blood glucose was high when it was checked at the clinic this morning before breakfast."
PN-S04-09.C: "It means you have excellent control of your diabetes, so you can keep following your current diet and medication plan."
PN-S04-09.D: "It measures the amount of ketones in your blood and tells us whether you are at risk for ketoacidosis."

PN-S04-11.A: "I'll take it at the same time every morning on an empty stomach."
PN-S04-11.C: "I'll report a racing heart, tremors, or trouble sleeping."
PN-S04-11.D: "I understand I'll need this medication for the rest of my life."

PN-S04-13.A: Provide extra blankets to keep the client warm and comfortable
PN-S04-13.C: Limit calorie intake to 1,200 calories a day to promote weight loss
PN-S04-13.D: Encourage caffeinated drinks such as coffee or cola for energy

PN-S04-15.A: Place the client flat without a pillow to keep the head and neck in straight alignment
PN-S04-15.C: Encourage the client to flex the neck forward and backward to prevent stiffness
PN-S04-15.D: Remove the tracheostomy tray from the room once the client is awake and talking

PN-S04-17.A: Encourage a high-sodium diet to help maintain the client's blood pressure
PN-S04-17.C: Restrict protein intake to reduce the workload on the client's kidneys
PN-S04-17.D: Encourage frequent visitors, including family members who have colds

PN-S04-18.A: "Take your hydrocortisone only on the days when you feel tired or weak, and skip the dose on days you feel well."
PN-S04-18.C: "Follow a low-sodium diet and avoid adding salt to your food, even on hot days when you sweat a lot."
PN-S04-18.D: "Stop taking your medication if you notice you are gaining weight, and call your provider at your next visit."

PN-S04-20.A: "You'll get used to it after a few more weeks, and it won't bother you as much then."
PN-S04-20.C: "Your parents will be very upset with you if you don't take your insulin."
PN-S04-20.D: "At least it's not something worse. Many teens have much bigger problems."

PN-S04-21.A: Decreased thirst since starting the medication
PN-S04-21.D: Urine output of 1,800 mL in 24 hours

PN-S05-02.A: "Collect the very first urine that comes out of the stream in the sterile cup, then finish urinating in the toilet."
PN-S05-02.C: "Touch the inside of the cup with your fingers to make sure it is completely dry before you use it."
PN-S05-02.D: "After you finish urinating into the toilet, scoop a sample of urine from the bowl into the cup."

PN-S05-06.A: As soon as the catheter tip enters the urethral opening, before urine flows
PN-S05-06.C: Before insertion, to check that the balloon inflates and holds its shape
PN-S05-06.D: After the drainage bag has collected the first 100 mL of urine from the bladder

PN-S05-08.A: "It will cure your bladder infection within a few days."
PN-S05-08.C: "Take it every day for 6 months to prevent infections."
PN-S05-08.D: "It may turn your urine a blue-green color while you take it."

PN-S05-10.B: "Limit your fluid intake to about 1 L a day from now on."
PN-S05-10.C: "Eat a very high-sodium diet and salt your food to taste."
PN-S05-10.D: "Avoid all calcium-containing foods, such as milk and cheese."

PN-S05-17.A: Restrict fluids to 500 mL/day to reduce the urge to void at night
PN-S05-17.C: Insert an indwelling catheter to keep the resident dry
PN-S05-17.D: Use adult briefs and change them once per shift as needed

PN-S05-18.A: "Tighten your abdominal and buttock muscles as hard as you can, hold for a few seconds, then relax. Repeat this daily."
PN-S05-18.C: "Do the exercises only while you are urinating, by starting and stopping the stream each time you go."
PN-S05-18.D: "Hold your breath while tightening the muscles, then breathe out slowly as you relax them again each time."

PN-S05-20.A: "Yes, she can split them as long as she washes her hands with soap and water right afterward."
PN-S05-20.C: "Yes, the medication is only harmful to her if she actually swallows some of it."
PN-S05-20.D: "It does not matter who handles the medication, as long as it is stored safely."

PN-S05-23.A: Encourage the client to drink 1 L of water quickly to help the bladder empty
PN-S05-23.C: Document the 50 mL void as adequate urine output for the first void
PN-S05-23.D: Restrict fluids until the client is able to void a larger amount
